hints: Recall the atomic number of copper (29) and how its electrons fill up to $3p^6$, then think about the unusual promotion that gives extra stability to a full $3d$ subshell.
Think about which electron is lost first when a transition metal forms a positive ion, the $4s$ or the $3d$ electron.
walkthrough:
Build up to argon and then face the copper exception**
Count out 29 electrons for Cu. Up to $1s^22s^22p^63s^23p^6$ you have used 18, leaving 11. You would expect $3d^94s^2$, but copper promotes one $4s$ electron into $3d$ to gain a full $3d^{10}$ subshell, which is extra stable. So you get $3s^23p^63d^{10}4s^1$ after the $1s^22s^22p^6$ core.

Remove the outer electron to make Cu+**
When transition metals ionise, the $4s$ electron is lost before any $3d$ electron because $4s$ is outer in the ion. So remove the single $4s^1$ electron from Cu to leave $3d^{10}$ with no $4s$ electrons: $1s^22s^22p^63s^23p^63d^{10}$.

hints: Recall that coordination number equals the number of coordinate bonds, and each monodentate $Cl^-$ forms one bond, so consider how many $Cl^-$ ligands give a linear shape.
Work out the overall charge by adding the $1+$ charge on copper(I) to the charges of the chloride ligands.
walkthrough:
Link linear shape to coordination number 2**
A linear complex has two ligands at $180^\circ$. Since $Cl^-$ is monodentate, each $Cl^-$ provides one coordinate bond, so two $Cl^-$ ions are needed: $Cl-Cu-Cl$.

Balance charges to get the formula**
Copper is present as $Cu^+$. Add two $Cl^-$: $(+1) + 2(-1) = -1$. So the complex is $[CuCl_2]^-$ carrying a single minus charge.
Final answer: $Cl-Cu-Cl$ linear with overall $1-$ charge, $[CuCl_2]^-$

hints: Count the number of water ligands in $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ to find the coordination number and the parent shape for six groups.
Recall the two characteristic bond angles in that six-coordinate shape, between adjacent and opposite ligands.
walkthrough:
Place six waters around copper**
$[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ has coordination number 6. Picture Cu in the centre with four $H_2O$ in a square plane, one above and one below. Each $H_2O$ bonds through O to Cu by a coordinate bond.

Label the octahedral angles**
This arrangement is octahedral. Neighbouring $O-Cu-O$ bonds are at $90^\circ$ and opposite $O-Cu-O$ bonds straight through Cu are at $180^\circ$. Mark both angles on the sketch.
Final answer: Octahedral diagram with central Cu surrounded by six $H_2O$ ligands, with $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ angles labelled.

hints: Recall what happens when a small amount of alkali or aqueous ammonia meets $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$, think colour and state of copper(II) hydroxide.
Write reaction 1 as the hexaaqua ion reacting with $OH^-$ (from $NH_3 + H_2O$) to give neutral $Cu(OH)_2$ plus water.
Recall the colour change when excess ammonia dissolves the precipitate by replacing ligands around copper.
Write reaction 2 as $Cu(OH)_2$ plus excess $NH_3$ forming the tetraammine complex $[Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{2+}$ plus $OH^-$.
walkthrough:
See dropwise ammonia as a base making a precipitate**
With a few drops, $NH_3(aq)$ acts as a base: $NH_3 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons NH_4^+ + OH^-$. The $OH^-$ deprotonates the hexaaqua ion and pulls out neutral copper(II) hydroxide. That is why you see a pale blue solid, $Cu(OH)_2$, separate from the blue solution.

Write the precipitation equation**
Show the full hexaaqua ion reacting: $$[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Cu(OH)_2 + 6H_2O$$ The charges balance ($2+ -2 = 0$) and six waters are released.

See excess ammonia as a ligand dissolving the solid**
In excess, $NH_3$ now acts as a ligand and replaces water and hydroxide around Cu. The blue solid redissolves to give a clear, intense deep blue solution containing the tetraammine complex.

Write the ligand exchange equation**
A correct form is: $$Cu(OH)_2 + 4NH_3 + 2H_2O \rightarrow [Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{2+} + 2OH^-$$ This shows four $NH_3$ molecules entering the coordination sphere to make $[Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{2+}$.

Final answer: reaction 1 observation: blue precipitate / blue solid
reaction 1 equation: $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Cu(OH)_2 + 6H_2O$
reaction 2 observation: deep / dark / royal blue solution
reaction 2 equation: $Cu(OH)_2 + 4NH_3 + 2H_2O \rightarrow [Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{2+} + 2OH^-$

hints: Think of the name for a reaction where one ligand takes the place of another in the coordination sphere without change in coordination number type.
walkthrough:
Recognise swapping of ligands**
$EDTA^{4-}$ pushes out the six water molecules from $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ and takes their place around $Cu^{2+}$. Whenever ligands swap like this it is called ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand substitution, displacement or replacement.
Final answer: ligand exchange / displacement / replacement / substitution

hints: Recall that $K_{stab}$ has the complex ion concentration on top and the product of the free hydrated metal ion and free ligand concentrations below, with water omitted.
walkthrough:
Build the equilibrium expression**
Write the equilibrium as $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + EDTA^{4-} \rightleftharpoons [CuEDTA]^{2-} + 6H_2O$. For $K_{stab}$ put the complex on the top and multiply the two reactants on the bottom, leaving out water because it is the solvent: $$K_{stab} = \frac{[[CuEDTA]^{2-}]}{[[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}][[EDTA]^{4-}]}$$
Final answer: $K_{stab} = [[CuEDTA]^{2-}] / [[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}][[EDTA]^{4-}]$

hints: Think about what a very large value such as $6.3 \times 10^{19}$ tells you about the position of equilibrium and the stability of the product relative to the reactant.
walkthrough:
Read the size of Kstab**
$6.3 \times 10^{19}$ is huge, so equilibrium lies far to the right. That means $[CuEDTA]^{2-}$ is very stable, much more stable than $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$, as expected for a polydentate chelate.
Final answer: stable / more stable than $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$

hints: Start from the general definition of any ligand in terms of lone pairs and the type of bond formed to the central metal ion.
Think what the prefix bi means for the number of such bonds each ethanedioate ion can form.
walkthrough:
Define the ligand bond**
A ligand is a species that donates a lone pair into an empty orbital on the central metal ion to form a dative or coordinate bond.

Add the meaning of bi**
Bidentate means each ligand does this twice. Ethanedioate, $C_2O_4^{2-}$, uses a lone pair on each of its two oxygen atoms to form two coordinate bonds to the same metal ion.

Final answer: donates lone pairs / forms dative / coordinate bonds to central metal atom / ion;
donates two lone pairs / forms two dative / coordinate bonds

hints: Count the total negative charge from four bidentate $C_2O_4^{2-}$ ligands plus the $4+$ charge on Zr to work out the overall charge of the complex.
Count the total number of coordinate bonds from four bidentate ligands and compare it with the six bonds needed for octahedral.
walkthrough:
Work out the formula**
Four $C_2O_4^{2-}$ give $4 \times (-2) = -8$. With $Zr^{4+}$: $(+4) + (-8) = -4$. So the ion is $[Zr(C_2O_4)_4]^{4-}$.

Check the coordination number**
Each ethanedioate is bidentate, so four ligands give $4 \times 2 = 8$ coordinate bonds. Octahedral means exactly six bonds arranged at $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. With coordination number 8 this complex cannot be octahedral.

Final answer: $[Zr(C_2O_4)_4]^{4-}$;
not octahedral because coordination number is 8 / is not 6, 8 dative bonds to Zr
